Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Delays' suggests a broad expectancy of external danger from uncertainty/delays, which fits poorly with the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; the rest of the profile centers on guilt, recall-based distress, and hypervigilance rather than delay-specific threat meanings.

issues.item: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For a patient whose trauma was accidentally injuring another, the appraisals presented otherwise focus on guilt, inadequacy, and permanent moral/personal change. A loss of trust in one's body usually implies prominent bodily injury, dissociation, panic-like symptoms, or functional impairment, none of which are represented elsewhere in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies.

vignette: Six months ago, Arthur was assisting his brother-in-law lower a heavy equipment crate into the basement of his own home. He had positioned himself to bear the load, but the strap slipped. The crate struck the man's thigh with a force that left a permanent scar and ended the brother-in-law's ability to return to his former work. The memory of that impact remained sharp, anchored by the sudden terror that had flooded him in the moment and the heavy guilt that followed. In the weeks since, those memories did not settle. They arrived without warning as sudden pieces-the sound of the strap giving way, the sickening thud, the clinical silence of the hospital waiting room-each fragment carrying the same terror and guilt he felt as if it were happening now. He could not dismiss them, nor could he predict when they would surface. His body adjusted to a new baseline. He sat awake long past midnight, convinced that drifting off would leave him defenseless. His muscles stayed knotted at the kitchen table and at his teller window. He was always watchful, scanning the bank floor for irregularities, for sudden movements. When he tried to rest at home, he was unable to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place. His shoulders remained raised, his breathing shallow, as though the basement were still echoing around him. He had come to believe his capacity for care had been compromised, that his body no longer trusted its own commands. He simply accepted that he would always be on guard. At the bank, the environment pressed against his routines. The teller line required him to face outward, hands on the counter, ready for the next transaction. The morning rush brought a steady stream of customers pressing forward, their voices overlapping with the hum of the vault door. When a regular customer reached across the polished wood to hand over an envelope, the unprepared touch sent a sharp jolt up his arms. He would set the transaction down, step back behind the glass, and wait until his pulse settled. Stress at the branch-long queues, a ringing phone, a supervisor asking about vault discrepancies-made his vision tunnel. He told himself he was managing, but at home, he flinched when his wife placed a hand on his shoulder. She was family, yet the closeness made his chest tighten. He stopped volunteering for weekend projects or community events. He watched himself struggle to keep pace with his old life, and every misstep confirmed his quiet conviction: he was inadequate. He did not think he would ever be the man he used to be. His reactions to the everyday world felt like proof that he was a lousy coper, that the damage was permanent. He had stopped trying to explain his exhaustion to his coworkers; he simply showed up, balanced his till with careful hands, and retreated. It was his wife who finally asked him to make an appointment, noting how he jumped at the closing of the bank's front door and how he barely ate with her anymore. Arthur went because he wanted the terror to stop, because he needed to know if he could ever feel safe in his own skin again. He was most afraid that the man who caused the injury would always be the only man he knew how to be, but he hoped, quietly, that someone might help him learn how to carry the weight without breaking.
